entries.title: India: Delhi braces for Cockroach protest amid strict curbs
entries.summary: The 'Cockroaches' are returning to Delhi to demand the resignation of India's election chief. Police have not authorized the protest, and heavy security arrangements are in place. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
India

India: Delhi braces for Cockroach protest amid strict curbs

Published October 10, 2026last updated October 10, 2026

The 'Cockroaches' are returning to Delhi to demand the resignation of India's election chief. Police have not authorized the protest, and heavy security arrangements are in place. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke to land in New Delhi shortly ahead of protest over alleged voter list manipulation
  • Around 43,000 police and paramilitary personnel are deployed in the capital, reports say
  • Traffic and transport disruptions are expected

Here is our rolling coverage of developments from India on Saturday, October 10:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section CJP's Abhijeet Dipke set to arrive in Delhi

CJP's Abhijeet Dipke set to arrive in Delhi

The Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) founder, Abhijeet Dipke, was due to land at Delhi's main airport on Saturday morning as the movement plans to hold a mass protest calling for India’s Chief Election Commissioner to step down over sweeping voter roll revisions, despite being denied permission by police.

Police and paramilitary forces, which local media reported numbered around 43,000 personnel, were deployed ahead of the protest. Multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocked the concrete-grey roads leading to the Jantar Mantar protest site.

On Friday, authorities also ordered the closure of more than 50 metro stations and canceled many trains bound for two major railway stations in the capital.

But India's top court later directed the government to not completely halt train services and said there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.

The Supreme Court stressed the "principle of proportionality," urging authorities to allow the transportation services in a regulated manner to avoid public inconvenience.

"Take measures only to the extent necessary to prevent them. But that does not mean you should use a hammer to kill a fly. That principle must be kept in mind," legal news website Bar and Bench reported the court as saying.

On Saturday, Dipke denounced the Modi government over extensive restrictions.

"Modi has accepted defeat even before our protest has begun," the CJP chief wrote on X ahead of his arrival in the capital.

"The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength, but of a leader terrified of his own people."

Skip next section Election protests: Pressure mounts on poll chief, challenge to PM Modi

Election protests: Pressure mounts on poll chief, challenge to PM Modi

The CJP is not the only group calling for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.

India's bloc of opposition parties, led by Congress' Rahul Gandhi, has been carrying out a sustained campaign against Kumar in recent days with its own protest marches.

The country has seen dramatic visuals emerge from Delhi's key corridor of political power, which showed leading opposition MPs, including Gandhi, being carried away to detention buses by uniformed police officials as they tried to dig their heels in.

The ire against India's election chief — the head of India's independent Election Commission — is turning into one of the biggest public and political challenges for Modi in his three-term rule. Opposition and critics allege that a mass deletion of tens of millions of voters from India's electoral rolls benefits Modi's Prime Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a charge the party denies.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi and this is a special edition of our daily India news blog.

As the early morning hours tick away, a countdown to a rally against India's top poll official over alleged voter list irregularities has begun in the heart of the world's largest democracy.

What's happening?

India's 'Cockroaches' are headed once again for Jantar Mantar —  the same protest site where the online satirical movement sprung to the mainstream as a youth-led pressure group in July after it forced the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's then education minister. 

The police have denied the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) permission to hold the demonstration but the group's leaders are heralding people from all over the country to converge at Jantar Mantar, calling the protest a "fundamental right".

A showdown between police and protesters seems imminent.

New Delhi, particularly its central areas, have essentially been turned into a fortress with a heavy security blanket — including thousands of paramilitary personnel — a rare mobile internet blackout, train cancellations and warnings from the police against any protest assembly.

The security arrangements come as memory is still fresh of a clash between youth demonstrators and police during the July Cockroach protest. Police used batons, tear gas and pellet-firing shotguns to disperse the agitating crowd. Several injuries were reported as the protesters alleged police brutality, while the police said it used force only after the protests stopped being peaceful.

We bring you all this and more. Stay with us as events unfold.

entries.title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
entries.summary: US weather authorities are warning of "life-threatening" storm surges on the Gulf Coast due to the Category 2 hurricane. Extreme winds, rising water levels and possible tornadoes are also on the radar.
entries.content:
October 10, 2026

US weather authorities are warning of "life-threatening" storm surges on the Gulf Coast due to the Category 2 hurricane. Extreme winds, rising water levels and possible tornadoes are also on the radar.

Hurricane Isaias has made landfall as a Category 2 storm near Destin, Florida, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Friday evening.

The storm is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.

What do we know about Hurricane Isaias?

The NHC warned of "life-threatening storm surge impacting the Gulf Coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash flooding spread inland."

The weather system is also bringing extreme winds, with a tornado watch issued for parts of Florida and southern Georgia.

Isaias was originally a strong Category 3 storm before making landfall. It later weakened to a Category 1 storm.

After the storm made landfall, the Florida Division of Emergency Management said the tornado watch for parts of North Florida has been extended until at least 6 a.m. local time Saturday (10 a.m. UTC).

The NHC said the hurricane has maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour (165 kilometers per hour).

Evacuations took place in coastal communities as the hurricane approached.

All flights at the Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport have been canceled due to the storm. Destin is in the panhandle region of northern Florida.

Florida, Georgia and Alabama have all declared a State of Emergency due to the extreme weather system.

US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said "emergency declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to #Isaias."

Florida Governor DeSantis urges residents to 'buckle down'

In a press conference, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis urged residents to "buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads."

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned those "thinking about using this storm's power outages and evacuations to break in, loot, or steal: don't even try it."

"During an emergency, these crimes become first-degree felonies, punishable by up to 30 years in prison," Uthmeier said.

According to power outage tracking site PowerOutage.com, roughly 480,000 customers altogether were without electricity as of Friday evening in Florida, Georgia and Alabama.

Alabama Governor Kay Ivey said Uber, Comcast and Home Depot have offered to help Alabamians during the storm. Uber, for example, is offering free round-trip rides to state-approved evacuation shelters in Mobile and Baldwin counties.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Mexico: Court finds three men guilty of murder of Australian, US surfers
entries.summary: The 2024 murders of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, shocked Mexico and drew international outrage.
entries.content:
October 10, 2026

The 2024 murders of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, shocked Mexico and drew international outrage.

A Mexican court on Friday convicted three men in the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, who were killed during a botched robbery which sparked international outrage.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico when they were shot dead in Baja California state.

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked during a suspected robbery. Their bodies were found days later, in a well, with gunshot wounds to their heads.

What was said in court?

The judge on Friday ruled that the three Mexican defendants had acted with premeditation. They are yet to be sentenced for the murders.

The prosecution has asked for an "exemplary sentence" of 210 years for each of the three convicted, even though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.

Debra Robinson, mother to the Australian brothers, burst into tears when the court passed the guilty verdict.

"While no verdict can ever bring back our boys or ease the heartbreak of losing them," the convictions marked "an important step towards justice and accountability," their father Martin Robinson said in a statement on behalf of the family.

Victim begged for mercy

Case prosecutors described the killings of the three surfers during the closing arguments on Thursday, by recalling the testimony of the girlfriend of one of the main suspects.

She had said that Rhoad had begged for his life while her boyfriend had bragged about "how beautifully" his victims cried before he robbed them.

The triple homicide shocked Mexico and drew international attention when it came to light.

Baja California is one of Mexico's most violent states, riddled with organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn't usually affect tourists.

entries.title: Trump weighs livestream execution amid bipartisan backlash
entries.summary: Donald Trump said he hasn't decided whether the execution of the Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed, after the Pentagon announced it would do so. The plan has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump weighs livestream execution amid bipartisan backlash

October 10, 2026

Donald Trump said he hasn't decided whether the execution of the Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed, after the Pentagon announced it would do so. The plan has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan "absolutely" deserves the death penalty by firing squad but told reporters he has yet "to make a determination" on whether it will be livestreamed.

"I don't really care how he goes, as long as he goes," Trump said, referring to Hasan.

What did Hegseth and the Pentagon say about Hasan's execution?

Trump's remarks comes a day after the Pentagon said it would livestream the execution of 56-year-old Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist who murdered 13 people and injured 32 others in Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

In a video shared by the Pentagon regarding the execution, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things."

Hasan is currently being held on death row in Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. His execution is slated for December 3.

He is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair after he was shot by an officer responding to the Fort Hood shooting.

JD Vance says he would not watch livestream of execution

US Vice President JD Vance, speaking to reporters in Cincinnati on Friday, also said he doesn't know whether the livestream is "actually going to happen."

"If it is shown publicly," Vance added, "I'm not going to be watching it." Vance is a devout member of the Catholic Church, which opposes the death penalty. 

"Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," the US vice president said.

Livestream plan faces bipartisan backlash

The Pentagon's plan to broadcast the execution has been met with a fierce backlash from within Trump's own Republican Party and the opposition Democrats.  

"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," said Republican Representative Austin Scott of Georgia.

Public executions are common in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan and the so-called Islamic State (IS) also engaged in public beheadings when the group controlled large swathes of Syria and Iraq in the 2010s. Iran is another country that carries out public executions.  

Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania said "an execution shouldn't be a livestreamed spectacle."

"The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment," he said in a statement posted on X. "Their pain deserves respect, not a public show."

Democratic Congressman Eugene Vindman of Virginia, who said he oversaw legal proceedings following the Fort Hood attack, said livestreaming Hasan's execution "is what terrorists and authoritarian regimes do. It's un-American."

Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said Pentagon chief Hegseth is "turning the Fort Hood execution into a gruesome inhumane spectacle."

The UN human rights office (OHCHR) also strongly condemned the ideaof a livestreamed execution, while the president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops called the plana "barbaric promotion of a culture of death."  

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Trump names new press secretary to succeed Karoline Leavitt
entries.summary: Trump has appointed Katie Zacharia to take over the White House press secretary role vacated by Karoline Leavitt. She assumes the role with Trump struggling with low approval ratings driven by the US war with Iran.
entries.content:
October 10, 2026

Trump has appointed Katie Zacharia to take over the White House press secretary role vacated by Karoline Leavitt. She assumes the role with Trump struggling with low approval ratings driven by the US war with Iran.

US President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Katie Zacharia will be the next White House press secretary, succeeding Karoline Leavitt.  

Zacharia is a 'loyal and brilliant supporter,' Trump says

In a post on his Truth Social network, Trump said it was a "great honor" to appoint Zacharia to the role, calling her a "loyal and brilliant supporter" and member of the Make America Great Again movement.  

Zacharia, a 42-year-old native of California, had been serving as Senior Communications Advisor to Truth Social. She had also earlier worked as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs at the Department of Homeland Security.

Zacharia, in a post on X, thanked Trump and said "his leadership is a blessing to this country."

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our country and communicating to the American people the major wins that the administration is making every single day," Zacharia said. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out."

Zacharia said her predecessor Leavitt was "fabulous" and that she set a "high standard" to meet for the press secretary job.

Will Zacharia follow Leavitt's combative approach?

Trump had announced that Leavitt would resign in August to spend more time with her young children and family.

Earlier this week, conservative-leaning broadcaster Fox News announced that Leavitt would provide commentary on the network starting from November 1.

Leavitt took a combative approach to questions from the White House press corps during her tenure as press secretary.

In January, she called a White House reporter a "left-wing hack" after a question regarding the fatal US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shooting of American citizen Renee Good in Minneapolis. She also had to defend Trump's controversial handling of the Epstein files and the ongoing Iran war.      

Leavitt managed to stay in the role for over 18 months — a long tenure for a high-stress job under a demanding president. During Trump's first term from 2017 to 2021, he had four press secretaries: Sean Spicer, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany.

Zacharia's tenure comes as Trump faces low approval ratings due to high energy prices amid the Iran war and the looming midterms on November 3, where the opposition Democrats are expected to make major congressional gains.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Schools crisis in France: Investment fails to inspire confidence
entries.summary: For weeks, schoolchildren in France have been protesting the failing education system. Compared to many other countries, France invests heavily in education but critics say that the funds are not distributed fairly.
entries.content:
October 9, 2026

For weeks, schoolchildren in France have been protesting the failing education system. Compared to many other countries, France invests heavily in education but critics say that the funds are not distributed fairly.

Rats in the toilets, leaking roofs, broken heating systems: Cellphone videos filmed by French schoolchildren and circulating on social media bear witness to the dilapidated infrastructure in many educational institutions across France.

At the Lycee Paul Eluard in the Parisian suburb of Saint-Denis, a center of the current protests, young people have reported that there are vermin in the building, and say burst pipes are a regular occurrence. In nearby Pantin, pupils complained that windows couldn't be opened, even when temperatures soared to 40 degrees Celsius (over 104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer.

Pupils also complain of overcrowded classrooms and frequently cancelled lessons.

The protests, which have erupted all over the country, show no sign of coming to an end. 

Problems of centralization

Yet, by EU standards, France invests a substantial amount in its education system — 6.7% of its GDP. The fact that this investment has not translated into a better learning environment may be partly attributable to the way responsibilities are divided.

The central government in Paris mainly deals with paying teachers, and setting national curricula. But the responsibility for maintaining school buildings lies with France's various levels of local government. For elementary schools, the administration responsible is the municipality; for "colleges" (lower secondary schools, ages 11–15) it is the wider department, and for lycees (upper secondary schools, ages 15–18) it is the region.

Depending on the region, the local authorities have different financial possibilities at their disposal, and must plan renovation projects themselves. Progress on making improvements is often very slow as a result. In addition, more than two-thirds of their budget is already allocated to staffing costs and pension payments, leaving relatively little room for investment.

Dilapidated infrastructure

Over 80% of elementary school buildings in France are more than 50 years old. An estimated 10 to 20% of all school buildings are considered to be in serious need of renovation. In many instances, politicians have been trying to address the problem. Ile-de-France, which covers Paris and the region surrounding it, approved a 10-year program of renovation and expansion for the period 2017 to 2027 at a cost of €6.6 billion ($7.4 billion).

According to the local authorities, two-thirds of upper secondary pupils now attend a new school, or one that has been renovated. But even after mold has been removed and roofs repaired, it is still rare for buildings to have effective protection against the summer heat. It is also a bitter irony that some buildings newly constructed at considerable expense, or renovated just a few years earlier, have been damaged in the recent protests.

Macron tried in vain to address problem

Imbalances are also evident in ongoing education expenditure. While France invests a comparatively large amount in upper secondary education, according to OECD calculations Paris spends less per primary school pupil than the average for industrialized countries. Education researchers emphasize that it is precisely these early years that lay the foundation for subsequent academic success.

The governments put in place by French President Emmanuel Macron have attempted to address this imbalance. Since 2017, class sizes in the first years of primary school have been halved in socially disadvantaged areas, and around 16,000 additional teaching posts created. 

Amid the ongoing protests, the government has said it now intends to recruit more than 3,000 supply teachers at short notice. French Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced that software would be used to identify schools that are in a particularly difficult situation.

These announcements are the government's first concrete response to the demands of the students, who have been demonstrating for almost two weeks now, calling for better facilities in secondary schools, more supply teachers and greater investment in the education system generally.

Increasing deficiencies

The latest scores for the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development’s (OECD) program for international student assessment (Pisa), which were published in September, illustrate the scale of the problems in the education system. According to the results, more than one in three 15-year-olds in France no longer achieve a basic level of competence in mathematics, for example.

Macron's reform of the upper secondary education system has also been criticized. The abolition of academic streaming in favor of specialist subjects selected by the individual was meant to give pupils greater freedom of choice. However, the large number of possible subject combinations make it difficult to timetable lessons. Students complain that they have too many free periods and longer school days.

The problems also extend to universities. A lecturer at a Paris university described a seminar attended by 50 students — so many that they have to fetch chairs from other rooms or sit on the floor. So far, she said, the university administration had done nothing about it.

Cancelled lessons

Compared with pupils in other EU countries, French schoolchildren have a high number of teaching hours per school year — on paper, at least. But the French Court of Accounts recorded that 9% of lessons at state colleges were cancelled in the 2023–24 school year. A study from the school year 2024–25 suggests that only around 12% of lessons cancelled at short notice are covered by other teachers.

The relatively low salaries of French teachers compared to those in neighboring countries are also a problem. OECD data shows that after 15 years in the profession teachers at lower secondary schools in France only earn about half as much as their German counterparts.

Broken promises of equality

France takes pride in its republican model of education, which is supposed to provide all children with equal opportunities, irrespective of their background. In reality, academic success in France is much more dependent on parents' socioeconomic circumstances than in many other countries. This is also apparent in that children from poorer families are far more likely to be affected by the cancellation of lessons.

The government's financial room for maneuver is currently restricted by the country's precarious budgetary situation. Although the draft budget for 2027 includes an additional €1.2 billion for the Ministry of Education, there are also plans to cut teaching posts, on the grounds that pupil numbers are falling.

Protests in the run-up to the presidential election

It's not just videos of dilapidated school buildings that are circulating on social media. As the discontent has spread, there is also footage of demonstrations where people carry placards with political slogans that have little to do with education policy. Some videos show burning barricades and clashes with the police, which faces accusations of usingdisproportionate force.

Some members of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party have associated themselves with the protesting students. Lawmakers have appeared at school blockades and shared related videos. The government has accused LFI of deliberately exploiting young people's anger for political purposes, an allegation that the party rejects.

With the French presidential election just six months away, the protests over the crisis in education are evolving into a power struggle.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Trump, Putin agree on deal to release Russian diesel to US, world markets
entries.summary: Russia will supply diesel to global markets in a bid to lower prices, US President Donald Trump has said. The move reverses years of pressure on the Russian economy following the invasion of Ukraine.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump, Putin reach deal to release Russian diesel to world

October 9, 2026

Russia will supply diesel to global markets in a bid to lower prices, US President Donald Trump has said. The move reverses years of pressure on the Russian economy following the invasion of Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump on Friday said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release Russian diesel to US and global markets.

The move, which aims to address rising fuel costs before the US midterm elections, marks a dramatic turnaround in US policy toward Moscow since the start of the war in Ukraine.

In a social media post, Trump wrote he had made a deal with Putin during a phone call that was supposed to be about a suspected plague outbreak in Russia.

What did Trump say?

According to Trump, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

Trump wrote that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that.

The US Treasury Department issued a temporary license that will allow Russian diesel to reach global markets through April 2027.

Trump's announcement follows his signing of a broad Russia sanctions law last month. The law is intended to clamp down on Russia’s energy sector and other areas that fuel its war against Ukraine.

What did Russian officials say?

Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian presidential envoy, reposted the Treasury Department's announcement on X, saying that "Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

Alexander Novak, Russia's Deputy Prime Minister, said that the country was ready to start supplying additional volumes of diesel to the United States and other countries from October.

He also said that Russia's exports are expected to rise further in November and December as refineries resume operations after maintenance.

Later, the Kremlin released a statement from Putin saying that, during their call, he and Trump had also devoted "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and had discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."

How has Ukraine reacted?

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has condemned the agreement, saying that any easing of sanctions without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious sign of "weakness."

"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy," he wrote on social media.

"Allowing Russia to ⁠sell ​petroleum products ​is an investment in a ​war that ‌must be ended, not prolonged. What ​is needed ⁠is real de-escalation with Russia ⁠on ​a reciprocal basis," the Ukrainian president stressed.

Zelenskyy added that Ukraine hopes the US will have a strong conversation with Russia: "A strong one, not a weak one."

Sanctions against Russia

Since its 2022 full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine, Moscow has been hit with rounds of sanctions by the United States and its Western partners.

But as the war has continued with no resolution in sight, Washington's commitment to that approach has appeared to waver.

Earlier this year, temporary US sanctions waivers that allowed the sale of Russian oil raised concerns because they could hinder efforts to deprive Moscow of funds for its war in Ukraine.

Last month, Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring diesel prices, and even publicly told Zelenskyy to stop the attacks. 

Trump's announcement on Friday came just as US, Ukrainian, and European officials were meeting in Miami for new diplomatic talks aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine.

According to US envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian, European, US and NATO representatives held "constructive" discussions in Miami, and agreed to continue diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.

What is behind Trump's deal with Putin?

According to Ines Pohl, the chief of DW's Washington D.C. bureau, the diesel deal is mainly about domestic politics.

With the midterms only weeks away, Trump is under heavy pressure over high energy prices. The deal allows him to show that he is taking action and appeal to voters who feel the rising cost of fuel directly, while the war in Ukraine seems far away.

Politically, that is significant: Trump is accepting a loosening of sanctions on Russia, even though Washington had actually wanted to increase pressure on Putin.

It also makes one thing crystal clear: when push comes to shove, Trump consistently chooses what benefits him personally over what Congress has decided.

He appears to be betting that, for many Americans, prices at the pump matter more in the end than the geopolitical consequences. Whether the promised deliveries will actually bring noticeable relief, however, remains doubtful.

Edited by: Sean Sinico, Karl Sexton

entries.title: Strong earthquakes shake Panama, buildings damaged
entries.summary: Panama's president has declared a "major disaster" after a series of tremors damaged buildings, briefly suspended flights and triggered a tsunami alert in Central and South America.
entries.content:
Panama

Strong earthquakes, aftershocks shake Panama

October 9, 2026

Panama's president has declared a "major disaster" after a series of tremors damaged buildings, briefly suspended flights and triggered a tsunami alert in Central and South America.

A powerful magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck Panama on Friday morning.

According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the quake's epicenter was located approximately 10 kilometers (6 miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama's southern tip.

The quake struck at a depth of 10 kilometers. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.

The USGS later reported that a second powerful earthquake, measuring 6.6 in magnitude, struck the country following a series of aftershocks.

The tremors were strongly felt in the capital Panama City, causing buildings to shake and sending people rushing into the streets.

"We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we're okay, though we're very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared."

Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino described the earthquake as a "major disaster" which had destroyed roads near the epicenter.

What do we know about damage?

Mulino did not say whether there were any casualties.

According to Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service, damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos.

Smith reported several injuries, as well as partial collapses and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage to the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel.

Meanwhile, local news outlets reported that the colonial-style Church of San Atanasio in Panama’s Los Santos province collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.

Tsunami warning lifted

The US Tsunami Warning System issued an alert stating that hazardous tsunami waves were possible along parts of the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Mexico within the next three hours.

The system also reported a tsunami threat to Hawaii. The warning was lifted later on Friday afternoon.

Initially, there were no reports of damage to the Panama Canal. The Panama Canal Authority stated that the waterway was operating as usual.

Tocumen International Airport in Panama City briefly suspended operations and activated evacuation protocols before reopening later on Friday afternoon.

Panama is located along the so-called "Ring of Fire," a line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur.

Edited by: Sean Sinico, Karl Sexton

entries.title: UAE: Omani Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack
entries.summary: A Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight into the terminal at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport, according to a UAE official.
entries.content:
United Arab Emirates

UAE: Omani Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack

October 9, 2026

A Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight into the terminal at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport, according to a UAE official.

The Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport in a suicide attack, according to the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor.

The statement released on Friday by Attorney General Hamad Saif al Shamsi and published by the state media did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing.

What has the investigation revealed so far?

According to the statement, UAE public prosecutors believe that the co-pilot's plan was inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US and aimed at "causing the greatest possible loss of life."

The investigation found that the suspect had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the flight route and airport. He had worked for several airlines in different countries, including Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, before joining Flydubai in January 2026.

The prosecutor's findings also showed that he met the professional and security requirements for employment.

These requirements included holding a pilot's license, providing a certificate of good conduct, and completing the necessary background checks.

"None of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot," according to the statement.

What happened on Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv?

On September 30, the Indian captain of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was injured when the co-pilot attacked him with an ax.

The captain opened the cockpit door, enabling passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and force an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Passengers described rushing the cockpit and fighting for control after the plane suddenly descended around 5,000 meters (17,000 feet).

Most of the passengers on board were Israeli. They have been hailed as heroes in Israel.

entries.title: China, EU reach deal to 'moderate' China's car exports to EU
entries.summary: An agreement between the EU and China would reduce exports of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid cars to the 27-member European bloc by up to 50%, according to the EU trade envoy.
entries.content:
October 9, 2026

An agreement between the EU and China would reduce exports of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid cars to the 27-member European bloc by up to 50%, according to the EU trade envoy.

European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic announced on Friday that China and the European Union had reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the EU by more than half.

This announcement followed two-day talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU's growing trade deficit with China.

Earlier, Sefcovic said this week's talks were the culmination of three months of intensive work.

What do we know about the EV deal?

According to Sefcovic, the deal would "moderate China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU."

He added that this opens the prospect of cutting China's exports by more than half, based on projections over a four-year period.

"By this step, we're actually preventing several millions of cars exports from China to the European Union," Sefcovic said.

Although he did not offer details on how the agreement will be implemented, Sefcovic said he believed the two sides had achieved a very good result.

What else was decided?

Sevcovic added the two sides also reached an agreement to reduce Chinese import duties on €4 billion ($4.5 billion) worth of EU exports, including car parts, olive oil and footwear.

They also agreed to simplify China's process for granting export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets.

The agreement will require approval from the leaders of all 27 EU nations, who will discuss the outcome at the start of their summit in Brussels on Thursday.

Rebalancing EU-China trade

According to UN Comtrade data, Chinese exports to the EU totaled $560 billion (€500 billion) last year, up from $517 billion in 2023. Exports to major economies, including Germany, Italy, Spain, and Poland, each rose approximately 10% from a year earlier. Shipments to Hungary increased by 43%.

Meanwhile, China imported $268.3 billion (€240 billion) worth of European goods last year, down from $269.4 billion the previous year. Purchases from Denmark, Ireland, and France led the way.

Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned lawmakers at the European Parliament that the trade gap had reached a tipping point. She said the EU would use all available tools to rebalance the relationship.
